articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope is about to crash to Earth. Where will it fall?
articles.summary: It's unclear at the moment exactly when and where the Swift observatory will plunge to Earth. But researchers definitely have their eyes peeled.
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

NASA's Swift space telescope is expected to crash back to Earth in the next few days.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will reenter Earth's atmosphere in an uncontrolled fashion, after a robotic rescue mission failed to boost the scope to a higher orbit.

Swift launched to Earth orbit back in November 2004. Over the next two decades, it studied gamma-ray bursts — the most powerful explosions in the universe — and other cosmic objects and events using a trio of telescopes: a Burst Alert Telescope (BAT), an X-Ray Telescope (XRT), and its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope (UVOT).

On Oct. 20, NASA reported that Swift's orbit had decayed to 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth and that the roughly 3,300-pound (1,500-kilogram) observatory was no longer able to compensate for the effects of the increased drag. It entered safe mode, followed by Swift's operations team at Pennsylvania State University sending a command to the spacecraft that effectively ended its operations ahead of its destructive and fiery nose-dive.

It's unclear at the moment exactly when and where Swift will plunge to Earth. But researchers definitely have their eyes peeled.

In physics fashion, for the most part, what goes up must come down — with more space hardware to follow.

Thanks to the growing surge in low Earth orbit constellations and technology refresh cycles, there are 10 times more objects reentering per year than there were just five years ago, said Darren McKnight, a senior technical fellow at LeoLabs, a company that keeps a watchful eye on what's going on above our planet.

"It is unfortunate that Swift was not 'reorbited,' but from a reentry hazard perspective it is a small portion of the stuff coming back in. The rub on this, of course, is that, while many people bemoan the reentry of more objects , I am much more upset about the rapid rate of abandoning massive objects above 400 miles [644 km]," McKnight told Space.com.

Swift will likely disintegrate sufficiently upon reentry to not pose a ground casualty hazard, McKnight said. However, the internal workings of the observatory's X-ray and optical telescope might survive, McKnight said.

Similar in view is Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at the U.K. precision-components supplier Accu Components.

"Once Swift falls to about 120 kilometers [75 miles], the end usually comes within a few minutes. The air in front of it heats up so much that the satellite will start to glow. Solar panels and antennas are typically the first to tear off, and at around 78 kilometers [48 miles], roughly eight times the height of a passing airliner, the main body breaks apart. Most of it will melt and vaporize," said Sladen.

While it isn't yet known exactly where any surviving pieces will land, Sladen noted that Swift's orbit only passes over a band within about 21 degrees of the equator.

"That band is mostly ocean, though it also crosses populated parts of Africa, South and Southeast Asia and Latin America," he said.

As for which parts are most likely to survive and reach ocean or ground, Sladen pointed out that most of Swift's body is aluminum , wiring and electronics, which melt away early in the reentry process. What reaches Earth is usually small, dense and heat-resistant, such as titanium, steel and glass.

"The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors. Its mask of around 52,000 tiny lead tiles will almost certainly melt. Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down — nothing recognizable as a telescope," Sladen said.

Sladen said that, at the current time, it appears that no detailed risk assessment has been published for Swift's fall.

"However, this does not mean NASA has not done the work," said Sladen.

"NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published," he told Space.com. "Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork."

Sladen added that there's far more focus on how a satellite's life ends these days than there was in the past.

"Many now carry enough propulsion to steer themselves into a remote stretch of ocean, or are built from materials designed to burn up completely, an approach called 'design for demise.' NASA and the European Space Agency limit the chance of anyone being hurt by a reentry to one in 10,000, and if a satellite can't meet that, it's expected to come down in a controlled way," said Sladen.

So, should people be worried about having a nasty run-in with Swift leftovers?

Sladen doesn't think so. NASA has said that harm to anyone on the ground is unlikely, and LeoLabs also describes the risk as very small. Most of the spacecraft will burn up, and any surviving pieces will most likely fall into the sea, he said.

"The real concern is the long-term trend. With more satellites being launched than ever, the number of uncontrolled reentries is growing, which is why designing satellites to come down safely matters more and more," Sladen concluded.

articles.title: Motociclista morre após bater em poste em Boa Vista | G1
articles.standfirst: Cleidton Martins Fernandes tinha 25 anos. Acidente ocorreu na madrugada desta segunda-feira (2), Dia de Finados, no bairro Cidade Satélite.
articles.summary: Cleidton Martins Fernandes tinha 25 anos. Acidente ocorreu na madrugada desta segunda-feira (2), no bairro Cidade Satélite.
articles.body:
Homem morre em acidente em avenida no bairro Cidade Satélite, em Boa Vista. — Foto: Reprodução/Redes sociais

Um motociclista identificado como Cleidton Martins Fernandes , de 25 anos, morreu em um acidente de trnsito na madrugada desta segunda-feira (2), no bairro Cidade Satélite, zona Oeste de Boa Vista .

O acidente ocorreu por volta de 4h30, na avenida Dom Aparecido José Dias. Quando a Polícia Militar chegou ao local, Cleidton estava caído no chão. Socorristas do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) tentaram reanimá-lo, mas ele não resistiu.

Testemunhas contaram à polícia que Cleidton seguia de moto pela avenida, no sentido Centro-bairro, quando perdeu o controle da direção e bateu no canteiro central . Em seguida, atingiu um poste de iluminação instalado no canteiro.

A pericia foi acionada e, após os trabalhos, o corpo foi removido pelo Instituto de Medicina Legal (IML). A motocicleta estava com o licenciamento em atraso e foi removida ao pátio credenciado do Departamento Estadual de Trânsito de Roraima (Detran-RR).

Leia outras notícias do estado no g1 Roraima .

articles.title: Scientists discover bacteria that use iron minerals to remove toxic sulphide, revealing a hidden process that may help limit aquatic dead zones
articles.summary: A bacterial process that uses iron minerals to remove toxic sulphide could help explain how oxygen-deprived environments regulate the compound naturally.
articles.body: A bacterial process that uses iron minerals to remove toxic sulphide could help explain how oxygen-deprived environments regulate the compound naturally. In a study published in Nature in August 2025, an international research team identified a metabolism called MISO, in which a bacterium uses solid iron minerals while oxidising sulphide to obtain energy for growth. The finding challenges the long-standing assumption that the reaction between sulphide and iron(III) oxide is purely chemical. The researchers demonstrated the process in a cultivated bacterium and identified the genetic potential for related activity across a wider range of microbial groups. The University of Vienna, whose researchers were part of the team, said the discovery could have implications for aquatic environments and may help prevent low-oxygen dead zones from expanding. The work also adds a biological link to scientists’ understanding of how iron, sulphur and carbon cycle through oxygen-free environments.How MISO bacteria use iron minerals to remove toxic sulphideThe study’s lead author, Song-Can Chen, worked with senior researchers Marc Mussmann and Alexander Loy, along with an international team. They named the process MISO, short for microbial iron oxide respiration coupled to sulphide oxidation. It involves microorganisms transferring electrons from sulphide to solid iron(III) oxide minerals, reducing the iron while oxidising sulphide. In oxygen-free environments such as marine sediments, wetlands and freshwater aquifers, microbial activity can produce hydrogen sulphide, a toxic gas with a distinctive rotten-egg smell. Iron(III) oxide minerals, including compounds found in rust, can react with sulphide. Until this research, scientific models generally treated the reaction as a non-biological chemical process that produces elemental sulphur and iron monosulphide. The researchers showed that microorganisms can also use this reaction to obtain energy for growth. In laboratory experiments, the team studied the bacterium Desulfurivibrio alkaliphilus, which used ferrihydrite, an iron(III) mineral, as an electron acceptor while oxidising sulphide. The biological process outpaced the equivalent abiotic reaction at low sulphide concentrations of about 50 micromolar.The results depended on the amount of sulphide supplied. When fed repeated small doses of about 50 micromolar sulphide, the culture converted more than 90% of it to sulphate, with negligible elemental sulphur formation. At higher doses, some elemental sulphur also accumulated. The researchers suggest that MISO can facilitate sulphate formation without requiring elemental sulphur disproportionation, although the bacterium may also use a 2-step route in which sulphide is initially converted into elemental sulphur. The experimental findings also have limitations. D. alkaliphilus was grown at pH 9.3, and the authors described its growth with ferrihydrite as restricted, with only 2 to 3 fold increases. Because the bacterium is an alkaliphile, its behaviour should not automatically be assumed to represent microbial activity across all marine sediments or other oxygen-poor environments.Could MISO bacteria help prevent aquatic dead zones from expanding?Oxygen-free sediments can allow toxic hydrogen sulphide to accumulate. NOAA says dead zones get their name because most marine life in them dies or moves away. Nutrient pollution is a major cause of human-driven dead zones. Excess nutrients can trigger algal blooms, and when the algae die and decompose, the process consumes oxygen in the surrounding water. Marc Mussmann said in the University of Vienna’s announcement that MISO bacteria remove toxic sulphide and may help prevent low-oxygen dead zones from expanding. The study did not test whether MISO affects dead zones in the field, so its potential contribution to these ecosystems remains uncertain. The researchers estimated that MISO could account for between 1% and 7% of total sulphide oxidation to sulphate in marine sediments worldwide. This is a first estimate, not a direct measurement of the process across the world's oceans. The paper titled Microbial iron oxide respiration coupled to sulfide oxidation links its potential global contribution to the substantial supply of reactive iron reaching the oceans through terrestrial runoff.What the discovery reveals about Earth's iron, sulphur and carbon cyclesThe study identifies a specific microbial capability that had not previously been demonstrated: gaining energy from solid-phase iron(III) oxides while oxidising sulphur compounds. This does not mean that all links between iron and sulphur metabolism were unknown. Some acidophilic microorganisms, for example, can couple elemental sulphur oxidation with the reduction of dissolved iron(III). MISO is distinct because it uses solid iron(III) oxides. The researchers also found that D. alkaliphilus fixes carbon dioxide while growing through MISO. This process, known as autotrophic carbon fixation, allows the bacterium to use inorganic carbon to build the material it needs for growth. It is different from photosynthesis, but demonstrates how microorganisms can build biomass using energy from chemical reactions rather than sunlight.The team’s genomic analysis identified the genetic potential for related iron-dependent sulphur processes across 37 bacterial and archaeal phyla. The researchers said this suggests that the capacity for MISO may extend beyond the bacterium they cultivated. However, identifying genetic potential across microbial groups is not the same as experimentally confirming the metabolism in every group. By identifying MISO, the study adds another mechanism to scientists’ understanding of how iron and sulphur interact in oxygen-free environments. Further research will be needed to establish how widely the process operates in natural settings and how much it contributes to sulphide removal in different marine, freshwater and terrestrial habitats.

articles.title: Google runs its first AI prompt in space and gets a poem back; CEO Sundar Pichai says: We've now successfully sent a command up to orbit, booted up the TPU, and...
articles.summary: Google has run its first AI prompt in space.
articles.body: Google has run its first AI prompt in space. Its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite, sent to orbit earlier this month, received a command from the ground, powered on one of its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), ran the prompt and returned a complete answer. The task was a haiku written from the perspective of a TPU orbiting Earth, with the world spinning beneath it.Sundar Pichai called it a “hello world” milestone, borrowing the phrase programmers use for the first test of any new system. The model behind the poem was Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, loaded onto the satellite before it left the ground, and it wrote about the blue planet below and starlight feeding its core. Engineers also had the satellite report on conditions around it, and Google says the spacecraft is working as expected.Power and radiation are the real tests for Google’s TPUs in orbitThere are four TPUs on board, but the satellite generates up to 1 kW, which is enough to run just one chip at a time for about 20 minutes. Those short windows also have to line up with ground station contact, which makes every exchange a scheduling exercise.Built with Planet, the satellite rode a SpaceX Falcon 9 on the Transporter-18 rideshare with more than 100 other spacecraft. Its chips had to survive forces of 50 to 100g on the way up, and engineers spent about three weeks checking every subsystem before sending the first prompt.The longer test is only starting. Cosmic rays and solar events can cause bit flips, where a value stored in memory changes on its own and corrupts data without tripping the usual checks. In a proton beam at UC Davis, Google’s Trillium TPUs took more radiation than a five-year mission would deliver, and ground tests suggest inference will suffer far less than training. Heat is the other concern. With no air in space, the chips shed heat through heat pipes and radiators rather than fans.Google plans two more Suncatcher satellites with laser links in 2027If this prototype holds up, two more satellites follow in 2027 with higher power and laser links between them. Google wants them flying close enough to split one large AI workload while drawing on sunlight that can yield up to eight times more solar power than on Earth.SpaceX’s planned orbital data centres will also use lasers but are expected to orbit too far apart to share processing, while Starcloud and Cowboy Space are building around single satellites. The economics still depend on SpaceX. Suncatcher’s own researchers estimate Starship would need about 1,800 flights to bring down the cost of reaching orbit enough for the plan to work in the 2030s.One haiku from one chip doesn’t settle that. The radiation and heat data this satellite sends back over the coming months will, and it decides whether those two satellites go up on schedule.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Dutch engineer built a car controlled by a goldfish swimming inside a water tank; his fish Blub steered the vehicle for 12.28 metres in one minute, earning a Guinness World Records title
articles.summary: A goldfish swimming inside a water tank has earned a Guinness World Records title after steering a motorised vehicle for 12.28 metres in just one minute.
articles.body: A goldfish swimming inside a water tank has earned a Guinness World Records title after steering a motorised vehicle for 12.28 metres in just one minute. The unusual invention was created by Dutch computer engineer Thomas de Wolf, whose pet goldfish, Blub, became the unlikely driver of a motion-sensing car that translates the fish’s movements into directions for its wheels. According to Guinness World Records (GWR), Blub and de Wolf achieved the record for the greatest distance covered in a motion-sensing vehicle by a goldfish in one minute. The attempt took place on the set of Italian television programme Lo Show dei Record in Milan on January 23, 2025, with the achievement reported publicly by Guinness in March 2026. Blub covered 12.28 metres (40 feet and 3.46 inches), comfortably exceeding the minimum distance of five metres required for the record.The vehicle was presented during the programme hosted by Gerry Scotti, with Guinness adjudicator Sofia Greenacre overseeing the attempt. After the record was confirmed, de Wolf received an official certificate and medal alongside his aquatic companion.How does a goldfish drive a car?The invention works through a motion-sensing camera mounted on the vehicle. Blub swims inside a transparent water tank fitted to a small, motorised, four-wheeled platform. When the fish moves towards one side of the tank, the camera detects its position and the system directs the vehicle to move in the corresponding direction. The setup effectively converts the fish’s movement inside the water into steering instructions for the car. It does not require Blub to operate a steering wheel, pedals or any conventional driving controls.The vehicle was designed to work with bright red fish because the camera can detect their movements more easily. Blub, an Italian goldfish owned by de Wolf, was therefore suited to the experiment. During the one-minute attempt, the car travelled in several directions. Reversing was permitted under the record rules, meaning all valid movement counted towards the total distance.Measuring the attempt required particular care because the vehicle did not simply travel in a straight line. Greenacre calculated the distance by counting how many times coloured marks on the wheels touched the ground as the car moved around. The procedure allowed the adjudicator to determine the total distance covered during the allotted 60 seconds.From a routine engineering job to a record-breaking experimentDe Wolf said the project began as a way to bring some fun into his everyday work as a computer engineer. “Normally, my job is quite monotonous, so I wanted to create something that would entertain people, turning my ‘serious’ job into something fun,” he said in a Guinness World Records news release.He also explained that the experiment was intended to demonstrate what could be achieved with technology, even when the application was not designed to solve an immediate practical problem.After the attempt, de Wolf joked about the challenge of explaining the achievement to his pet. “How am I going to explain to Blub now that he has a world record title?” he said after receiving the certificate.While the experiment was designed primarily as an entertaining engineering project, it also raised the possibility of adapting similar motion-sensing technology for more practical uses. During the television programme, host Scotti suggested that the technology might one day help people with physical impairments. De Wolf expressed interest in exploring that possibility.“I would love to maybe one day be able to help people with mobility issues,” he said, according to Guinness World Records. For now, Blub’s achievement remains an unusual combination of pet ownership, engineering and record-breaking ambition. The goldfish may not understand the significance of the title, but its movements carried the vehicle more than twice the minimum required distance and secured an official place in the Guinness World Records.

articles.title: Los castores regresan al lago Ness por primera vez en 500 años: serán liberados para ayudar a restaurar los humedales y hacer frente a la crisis climática
articles.standfirst: Estos animales juegan un papel fundamental para la fauna y biodiversidad de la zona
articles.summary: Estos animales juegan un papel fundamental para la fauna y biodiversidad de la zona
articles.body: Trees for Life y Beaver Trust, dos organizaciones especializadas, se van a encargar de que, a lo largo de los próximos tres años y comenzando por este mismo mes de noviembre, se van a liberar hasta 15 grupos familiares de castores en las inmediaciones del lago Ness. Con esta iniciativa, el objetivo es luchar contra la crisis climática, mejorar los humedales, beneficiar a la fauna silvestre y la biodiversidad. El papel de los castores en el planeta es mucho más importante de lo que muchos creen, ya que estos animales crean presas y canales que ayudan a reconectar ríos, humedales y llanuras aluviales. Esto, a su vez, mejora la vida silvestre y genera un impacto menos lesivo por el cambio climático: sequías, incendios e inundaciones. Otra motivación de la reintroducción de esta especie en el lago Ness es que, al trabajar sobre la zona, mejorará el ecoturismo, puesto que ayudará al patrimonio natural y cultural. Para evitar que los curiosos molesten a los castores una vez se inicie su liberación, se informará de aquellos lugares en los que no se debe perturbar su vida y dejar que estos animales vivan y se desarrollen en paz. NatureScot, una agencia medioambiental, considera que los castores van a “mejorar significativamente” la diversidad en los alrededores del río. Además, aumentará la población de castores en Escocia, que es otra de las prioridades en la estrategia nacional lanzada en 2022 y que se alargará hasta el año 2045. “Los castores son aliados clave para afrontar las crisis interconectadas del clima y la biodiversidad a las que nos enfrentamos todos, por lo que este exitoso resultado nos brinda una verdadera esperanza para el futuro”, indica Alan McDonnell, responsable de Trees for Life. “Los castores pueden aportar muchos beneficios a la naturaleza y a las personas, creando hábitats como estanques y humedales donde prosperan otras especies, además de moderar los flujos de agua en épocas de inundaciones y escasez hídrica”, añade Robbie Kernahan, director de la fauna silvestre de NatureScot.

articles.title: In 2006, scientists discovered a white mineral in Serbia whose chemical composition almost matched Superman's fictional Kryptonite; they named it Jadarite,  it lacked just one element, one which gave Kryptonite its green colour
articles.summary: A mineral found in Serbia has an unusual connection to Superman's fictional Kryptonite.
articles.body: A mineral found in Serbia has an unusual connection to Superman's fictional Kryptonite. Known as Jadarite, the white mineral has almost the same chemical composition as the substance that weakens the superhero in comics and films. First discovered in 2004, it attracted international attention in 2007 when scientists identified its similarity to Kryptonite. Nearly two decades later, researchers at London's Natural History Museum have found that the mineral could also become an important source of lithium for electric vehicles in Europe.Unlike the glowing green Kryptonite shown in Superman stories, Jadarite is white, powdery and not radioactive. Its resemblance to the fictional substance is limited to its chemical composition. However, scientists are now more interested in the mineral's potential use in batteries than its connection to the superhero.A study discussed by the Natural History Museum last year examined the conditions under which SJadarite formed and why it has so far been found in only one part of Serbia. The researchers believe that understanding these conditions could help scientists identify other locations where the mineral might exist.The findings also raise questions about whether Jadarite should be mined. Although the Serbian deposit contains a large quantity of lithium, local opposition has prevented mining operations from going ahead.Jadarite's connection to KryptoniteThe connection between Jadarite and Kryptonite emerged when mining company Rio Tinto submitted a drill-core sample from Serbia to Chris Stanley, a mineral expert at London's Natural History Museum.Stanley examined the mineral and searched online for its chemical formula, sodium lithium boron silicate hydroxide. According to an Associated Press report published by CBS News, the search produced an unexpected result. The same scientific name appeared in the 2006 film Superman Returns.In the film, Superman's enemy Lex Luthor steals a piece of Kryptonite from a museum. The rock is displayed with a description that closely matches the chemical composition of the mineral found in Serbia.Speaking in 2007, Stanley explained how he made the connection. "Towards the end of my research I searched the Web using the mineral's chemical formula, sodium lithium boron silicate hydroxide, and was amazed to discover that same scientific name written on a case of rock containing kryptonite stolen by Lex Luthor from a museum in the film 'Superman Returns,'" Stanley said.The discovery attracted attention because of the similarity, although the real mineral does not possess the fictional properties of Kryptonite.The mineral was subsequently named Jadarite, after the Serbian region where it was discovered. At the time, the Natural History Museum said scientists typically identified around 30 to 40 new minerals each year, many occurring only as tiny grains visible under a microscope.Why Jadarite has been found only in SerbiaScientists have since tried to understand why Jadarite is so rare. Research led by Francesco Putzolu and colleagues at the Natural History Museum examined the geological conditions responsible for its formation.Their findings, published in Nature Geoscience, suggest that Jadarite developed through an unusual combination of volcanic activity and highly alkaline soda lakes that existed in the region up to 16 million years ago.These conditions had to occur together for the mineral to form. Researchers believe this explains why Jadarite has not been identified elsewhere, despite other locations having similar chemical environments.“We’ve likened it to baking a cake,” explained Professor Richard Herrington, a co-author of the research. “We need just the right ingredients and the just the right conditions and suddenly this mineral forms,” he added.Herrington said the combination of geological conditions appeared to have occurred by chance. Understanding this process could help researchers search for Jadarite deposits in other regions. For now, however, the mineral has only been found in Serbia's Jadar Valley.Use in Europe's electric vehicle industryBeyond its connection to Superman, Jadarite has attracted scientific and commercial interest because it contains lithium, an important material used in electric vehicle batteries.According to the Natural History Museum, Jadarite contains lithium in quantities comparable to spodumene, a mineral commonly mined for lithium. It also contains commercially valuable concentrations of boron.Researchers believe the Serbian deposit could become a major source of lithium because of its size and the relative ease with which the mineral can be processed.“There’s nearly a hundred million tonnes of Jadarite in the deposit,” Herrington said. “If mining is given the go-ahead this could be nine tenths of all the lithium Europe needs for its electric vehicles, so it’s pretty substantial.”However, the possibility of extracting the mineral has faced strong opposition from local communities. Plans to develop a mine and processing facility have remained controversial, preventing the deposit from being exploited.Scientists say this reflects a wider challenge in obtaining the raw materials needed for cleaner energy technologies while addressing concerns surrounding mining.The researchers hope that a better understanding of Jadarite's formation will help locate other deposits and contribute to discussions about its possible future use.

articles.title: Cornell researchers tested sheep grazing under New York solar panels for three years; at two sheep per hectare, beneficial insects rose 38% versus mowing, while honey bees increased 83%
articles.summary: Solar farms could offer more than clean energy.
articles.body: Solar farms could offer more than clean energy. A three-year study by Cornell University researchers in New York has found that allowing sheep to graze beneath solar panels may also benefit insects, including bees and lady beetles, when the animals are kept at the right density. The findings, published in Environmental Research Letters on October 7, 2026, suggest that using sheep to manage vegetation can deliver ecological benefits alongside renewable power generation. Cornell Chronicle and science news outlet Phys.org reported the findings on October 14. At a grazing density of two sheep per hectare, researchers recorded 38% more beneficial insects than in plots where vegetation was controlled by mowing. Honey bees accounted for much of the increase, with their abundance rising by 83%. However, the study also found that increasing the number of sheep did not necessarily produce better results for insect populations, highlighting the importance of balancing vegetation management with biodiversity.How sheep grazing can benefit solar farmsThe research was conducted at Cornell University's Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. Over three years, researchers examined how different sheep stocking rates affected insect populations and vegetation around solar panels.Solar farms need regular vegetation management because tall grass and other plants can shade panels or interfere with their operation. Mowing is one way to control growth, but grazing sheep offers an alternative that allows land to serve two purposes at once: generating electricity and supporting agricultural activity.This approach, known as solar grazing, is part of a broader practice called agrivoltaics, which combines solar energy production with agriculture on the same land. Cornell's earlier research into solar grazing has explored how the approach can help farmers maintain productive livestock operations while reducing the need for conventional vegetation management.The latest findings add another dimension to the practice by examining how grazing intensity affects beneficial insects. Rather than treating sheep management and pollinator conservation as separate concerns, the researchers assessed how both could be accommodated within the same solar installation.Why the number of sheep mattersThe researchers found that the ecological benefits depended on how many sheep grazed in a given area. At four sheep per hectare, beneficial insect numbers were similar to those recorded in the mowed control plots, although vegetation management was more effective than at the lower stocking rate. At eight sheep per hectare, the sheep were most effective at controlling vegetation, and flock health remained high. However, honey bee abundance fell by 45%, illustrating a potential trade-off between maintaining grass and supporting insect populations.These findings suggest that there is no single grazing density that maximises every benefit. A smaller flock may be better for beneficial insects, while a larger flock can provide more effective vegetation control. The appropriate stocking rate will depend on the priorities of farmers and solar farm operators, as well as local environmental conditions.The economic opportunity for sheep farmersThe ecological research was accompanied by a separate Cornell study examining how solar grazing can become a more viable business for sheep farmers. Published in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management on September 28, 2026, the research introduced a spreadsheet-based decision-support tool designed to help farmers manage flock sizes, costs, sales and expected vegetation at individual solar sites.The model can help farmers determine how many sheep they need to meet a solar operator's vegetation-management requirements while accounting for the costs of acquiring and maintaining their flock. It can also help solar developers structure contracts that better reflect farmers' operational needs. For sheep farmers, these arrangements can provide a source of income beyond selling meat and wool. Solar grazing contracts may also give them access to land and animal feed, helping them expand their businesses without having to purchase additional grazing property. The model has already been incorporated into the onboarding process of United Agrivoltaics, a company working with sheep farmers and solar installations.A different way to think about renewable energyThe findings come as solar development continues to raise questions about how land can be shared between energy production, agriculture and conservation. Solar grazing offers one possible solution, allowing sheep to control vegetation while keeping land in agricultural use. However, the Cornell study does not suggest that grazing alone will automatically increase biodiversity at every solar farm. Its results demonstrate that management decisions, particularly stocking density, can influence the balance between vegetation control and insect habitat.The research provides a practical starting point for farmers, developers and local authorities considering how to make solar installations more environmentally beneficial. By choosing grazing rates carefully, they may be able to combine renewable electricity generation with viable farming operations and improved conditions for beneficial insects. As the use of solar energy expands, the challenge will be to ensure that these installations deliver more than electricity. Cornell's findings suggest that, with thoughtful management, the land beneath solar panels can also support farming and contribute to healthier ecosystems.

articles.title: New Hampshire has closed 20 acres of Great Bay to shellfish harvesting for five years starting November 1, protecting two oyster restoration sites as scientists work to rebuild reef habitat near Nannie Island
articles.summary: Oyster reefs play a crucial role in supporting underwater ecosystems, providing shelter to marine species while also maintaining the quality of the
articles.body: Oyster reefs play a crucial role in supporting underwater ecosystems, providing shelter to marine species while also maintaining the quality of the surrounding water. In New Hampshire’s Great Bay, efforts to restore these reefs have been announced in recognition of their importance. On October 29, 2026, the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department announced that 20 acres of Great Bay would be closed to shellfish harvesting from November 1, 2026, through October 31, 2031. Through this five-year effort, the goal is to continue restoration without disturbance by placing specific sections of the estuary off-limits to shellfish harvesting.This decision has come about in collaboration with The Nature Conservancy and the University of New Hampshire. The closure covers two separate restoration sites, one measuring 5 acres near Woodman Point and another spanning 15 acres near Nannie Island. The existing natural oyster reefs remain open to recreational oyster harvesters.The five-year closure will remain in effect until October 31, 2031. Rather than closing the entire surrounding waterway, the department has restricted harvesting within specific areas where restoration is taking place.Why Great Bay's oyster reefs need protectionBut a major question remains: why is this move necessary to protect oyster reefs? The effort underway is part of a much larger attempt to address the decline of oyster reefs in the Great Bay area. The eastern oyster, especially, has historically been regarded as an indispensable part of the region's marine life. Information from The Nature Conservancy further supports this, as Great Bay may have supported as many as 1,000 acres of living oyster reefs back in 1970. However, more than 90% of these oysters were lost over time due to pollution, harvesting and disease.The loss of these reefs had consequences beyond the decline of a single shellfish population. Oysters are filter feeders; they draw water over their gills and remove microscopic algae and suspended particles as they feed, thus clearing the water. An adult oyster can filter upwards of 50 gallons of water a day. This process, beyond clearing the water, can also support the recovery of eelgrass beds, which provide important habitats for marine life.Oyster reefs themselves create habitats that other species depend on. As oysters grow, their shells accumulate and form complex underwater structures, creating spaces where fish, crabs and other marine organisms can find shelter. These reefs can also act as natural barriers along the coast, helping reduce wave force, stabilise shorelines and limit erosion. Their disappearance, therefore, affects several interconnected parts of the ecosystem, making their restoration important to the wider health of Great Bay. How scientists are working to rebuild the reefsThe restoration work around Nannie Island has involved more than simply placing oysters back into the water. It has brought together researchers, conservation organisations and local oyster farmers, who have been contributing to efforts to rebuild reef habitats over several years.These oysters do more than increase the number of shellfish in the water. Their shells provide a surface on which oyster larvae, known as spat, can settle and develop, helping new generations of oysters establish themselves. The Nature Conservancy's restoration programme involves placing oyster larvae on shells, raising juvenile oysters and eventually introducing them to restored reef sites.The Nature Conservancy's restoration programme also relies on scientific assessments to determine where reef-building efforts should take place. Historical reef maps, water-quality information and community input are considered before selecting sites, while monitoring plays an important role in helping researchers assess oyster survival, growth and reef health. Giving the ecosystem time to recoverThe new closure is another step in this longer restoration process. By keeping harvesting activities out of the two designated areas for five years, New Hampshire is allowing the restoration sites to develop while researchers and conservation partners continue their work. The restriction does not mean that all oyster harvesting in Great Bay has stopped, nor does it mean that the natural reefs surrounding the restoration sites are being closed.When an ecosystem has witnessed a decline as major as that in Great Bay, the need for action becomes greater. The restoration efforts over the next five years can potentially strengthen the reef structures. Both the time and effort invested can help the underwater habitat become healthier. While the success of this effort cannot be determined just yet, it does highlight a major step towards conserving the oyster reefs and their population.

articles.title: New York volunteers spent seven years preparing six 175-pound reef balls for Eastchester Bay; weeks after the October 2026 installation, divers spotted fish, crabs and shrimp sheltering among oyster-covered structures

articles.body: Volunteer efforts and years of research aimed at restoring the oyster population in the waters of Eastchester Bay have, after seven years, come to fruition. On October 9, 2026, volunteers with City Island Oyster Reef carried six concrete reef balls into the bay, near Delmour's Point, marking the organisation's first installation of permanent reef structures. According to the Bronx Times, through sustained research and planning near City Island, volunteers have now begun installing permanent artificial reef structures to encourage the return of native oyster populations.Each structure weighed approximately 175 pounds, or 79 kilograms, making the installation a huge undertaking for the volunteers and their families, who waded into the water to place them. The installation of the reef balls was therefore a memorial ceremony in itself.The organisation, which was founded in 2019, has spent much of this time studying the conditions around City Island to understand whether native oysters could survive and eventually establish a self-sustaining reef. Volunteers and researchers had been involved in monitoring water quality in the face of challenges posed by sewage and stormwater runoff. Underwater surveys were therefore conducted to examine the seabed and identify locations that could provide the right conditions and environment for oysters to attach themselves and grow.The reef balls themselves had been kept at Cornell Cooperative Extension's marine hatchery in Southold since June 2026, where they were seeded twice with oyster larvae before being transported to City Island. The region where this project is taking place is also an informed choice, as the Bronx Times reports that Save the Sound's 2026 beach ratings gave failing grades to several locations, including American Turners New York, White Cross Fishing Club and Trinity Danish Young People's Society, because of concerns about bacterial contamination in the water.Why prepare reef balls?Reef balls offer a firm, submerged surface on which young oysters can settle and attach themselves, and as more oysters settle and develop, they begin forming clusters across the structures. Eventually, these oyster-covered structures can develop into living reefs that can provide shelter for other marine life, including fish, shrimp and crabs. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), oyster reefs provide shelter and feeding grounds for a variety of aquatic species, including fish, crabs, shrimp and other invertebrates.Oysters are particularly important to coastal ecosystems because of the way they feed. Oysters are filter feeders, meaning they draw water through their bodies, removing algae and other organic particles in the process. As they filter suspended particles from the water, they can potentially improve water clarity, providing a foundation for other organisms to settle. A developing oyster reef can therefore support several interconnected forms of marine life, rather than simply increasing the number of oysters in a particular area.While the presence of an oyster reef cannot independently eliminate sewage pollution or make contaminated water safe for swimming, it can, according to the report, contribute to restoring the marine habitat and filtering the surrounding water.Monitoring the reef and its marine lifeCity Island Oyster Reef has already been involved in monitoring several sites around the island, studying oyster growth, survival and the presence of other marine organisms. Its research and monitoring work has documented more than 51 species, including fish, invertebrates and algae, around its oyster monitoring sites.The project, since its inception, has already witnessed significant achievements, with the organisation's volunteer scuba diving team observing the presence of fish, crabs, shrimp and healthy oysters while inspecting the reef. Moreover, researchers have also counted oysters on two reef balls, comparing one with an open bottom against another with a closed bottom. The team also employed a technique called photogrammetry, which involves taking photographs from different angles to create detailed three-dimensional images.The October installation has also carried personal significance for the people who have taken part in bringing this project to life. The six reef balls were also placed in dedication to the memory of eight contributors who had supported the organisation's efforts. Their names were engraved on identification tags, which were then attached to the structures. Family members and volunteers also gathered to mark this special occasion and pay tribute to those who have been unflagging in their efforts to restore an environmentally safe marine ecosystem that is now taking shape beneath the water.
